# Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium: Eider Duck exercise

```{r}
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE)
```

We assume here that you have already followed the previous exercise on hedgehog spine colouration.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| label: fig-eider-ducks
#| fig-cap: "A male and female Eider. Source: RSPB"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures", "eider-ducks-m-f.jpg"))
```


An iconic study by Milne and Robertson [-@milne1965] used protein electrophoresis to show that a population of Eider ducks (Somateria mollissima) around the Ythan estuary of north-east Scotland has two codominant alleles of a gene that codes for egg-white protein. One variant of the protein migrates quickly through the gel used in the electrophoresis and one migrates slowly. In the following, we use F to denote the allele that codes for the fast protein and S for the one that codes for the slow.

By studying the frequencies of these alleles and comparing the results with the expectations under Hardy-Weinberg (HW) equilibrium, they could establish whether this population of Eiders met the assumptions of HW - large population, random mating, no mutation, no natural selection, no gene flow in or out of the population.


They studied 67 individual ducks and found

| Genotype | Phenotype                                          | Frequency |
|:---------|:---------------------------------------------------|:----------|
| FF       | Fast moving ovalbumin variant synthesised          | 37        |
| FS       | Fast and slow moving ovalbumin variant synthesised | 24        |
| SS       | Slow moving ovalbumin variant synthesised          | 6         |

**Is this population of ducks in Hardy-Weinberg equlibrium?**

## Calculation of frequencies of F and S alleles.

Let us use *p* to denote the frequency of the F allele and *q* to denote the frequency of the S allele. 

:::{.callout-note title="Frequency"}
In this context, 'frequency' means proportion. So, if an allele of a gene had a frequency of 0.64 that would mean that 64% of the alleles of that gene were of that type. When there are two alleles of a gene, their frequencies are commonly referred to as  p and q, with p usually denoting the dominant allele, if there is one. The frequencies of all the alleles of a gene must add up to one. 
:::

We know

$$
\begin{align*}
p&=\frac{\text{Total number of F alleles}}{\text{Total number of alleles}}\\
&=\frac{2 FF + FS}{2N}\\
&=\frac{2\times 37 + 24}{2\times 67}\\
&=\frac{98}{134}\\
&=0.7313
\end{align*}
$$

We know that $q = p-1 = 0.2687$, but let's caclulate it here from first principles just as we did for p, as a check on our arithmetic:

$$
\begin{align*}
q&=\frac{\text{Total number of S alleles}}{\text{Total number of alleles}}\\
&=\frac{2 SS + FS}{2N}\\
&=\frac{2\times 6 + 24}{2\times 67}\\
&=\frac{36}{134}\\
&=0.2687
\end{align*}
$$

Note that $p + q = 1$, as they must. There are two alleles, so their respective proportions must add up to one.

## Calculate expected number of each genotype under H-W

| Genotype | Expected frequency |   |   | Expected number *E* |   |   |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| FF | *p*^2^ | = 0.7313 x 0.7313 | = 0.5349 | *N* x *p*^2^ | = 67 x 0.5349 | = 35.84 |
| FS | 2 *pq* | = 2 x 0.7313 x 0.2687 | = 0.3930 | *N* x 2 *pq* | = 67 x 0.3930 | = 26.33 |
| SS | *q*^2^ | = 0.2687 x 0.2687 | = 0.07218 | *N* x *q*^2^ | = 67 x 0.07218 | = 4.84 |


Note that $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$, as must also be the case. There are three genotypes, so their respective proportions under HW (or any other scenario) must add up to 1.

## Compare observed and expected numbers

| Genotype | Observed number | Expected number |
|:--------:|:---------------:|:---------------:|
|   FF.    |       37        |      35.84      |
|   FS.    |       24        |      26.33      |
|   SS.    |       6\.       |      4.84.      |

These look very similar. It looks as though the duck population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. To check, we carry out a Chi-square goodness of fit test, with one degree of freedom

```{r, echo = TRUE}
# observed counts
observed <- c(AA = 37, Aa =  24, aa =  6)   
N <- sum(observed)

# allele frequencies
p <- (2 * observed["AA"] + observed["Aa"]) / (2 * N)
q <- 1 - p
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cat("Allele Frequencies:\n")
cat(sprintf("p (F allele) = %.4f\n", p))
cat(sprintf("q (S allele) = %.4f\n", q))
cat(sprintf("p + q = %.4f\n\n", p + q))
```
```{r, echo = TRUE}
# Expected genotype frequencies under HW
expected_frequencies <- c(p^2, 2 * p * q, q^2)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cat("Expected genotype Frequencies:\n")
cat(sprintf("p^2 (FF genotype) = %.4f\n", p^2))
cat(sprintf("2pq (FS genotype) = %.4f\n", 2*p*q))
cat(sprintf("q^2 (SS genotype) = %.4f\n", q^2))
cat(sprintf("p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = %.4f\n\n", p^2 + 2*p*q + q^2))
```


```{r, echo = TRUE}
# expected counts
expected <- N * c(p^2, 2 * p * q, q^2)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cat(sprintf("Observed counts: "))
cat(sprintf("%.0f", observed))
cat(sprintf("\n\n"))
cat(sprintf("Expected counts: "))
cat(sprintf("%.2f", expected))
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
# calculate chi-squared (X2 )statistic
X2 <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cat(sprintf("χ² statistic: %.4f\n", X2))
```

```{r, echo = TRUE}
# calculate p-value
p_value <- pchisq(X2, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
cat(sprintf("p-value: %.4f\n", p_value))
```

@fig-chi-square-pdf-eider shows what this results looks like:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| label: fig-chi-square-pdf-eider
#| fig-cap: "A Chi-square probability density function for one degree of freedom. The total area under the curve is one and the area under it between any two values of $\\chi^2$ is the probability of $\\chi^2$ being in that range. The area shaded blue is the area under the curve to the right of the $\\chi^2$ value of 0.524. This is the probsbility of getting a $\\chi^2$ value of 0.524 or greater, and thus is the probability of getting genotype numbers as different, or more different, from the Hardy-Weinberg predictions as the ones we got"

ggplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,8), breaks = seq(0,8,1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1.1), breaks = seq(0,1,0.5)) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dchisq,
    args = list(df =1),
    geom = "area",
    xlim = c(0.524, 8),
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_function(fun = dchisq, args = list(df = 1), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = bquote("Test statistic"~(chi^2)), y = "Density") +
  # scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,12), breaks = seq(0,12,1)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.524, y = 0, xend = 0.524, yend = 1.0), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  # scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = 1.3, y = 0.07, label = "p-value = 0.469", size = 3) +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = .6, y = 1.0, label = "chi^2 == 0.524", parse = TRUE, hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = 4, y = 0.6, label = "Total area under the curve = 1\n  Area shaded blue = 0.469\nThis is the p-value") +
  theme_cowplot()
```

## Conclusion

The Chi-square goodness of fit test gives a p-value of 0.469. This is much greater than 0.05, so we do not reject the null hypothesis, which is that the duck population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. We would normally expect this for any large outbreeding population. if mutation or natural selection are occurring (they must be, at some pace or other) then their effects must be small.



```{r, include = FALSE}
# Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium Chi-Squared Test
# Eider duck protein polymorphism data

# Observed genotype counts
obs_FF <- 37
obs_FS <- 24
obs_SS <- 6
N <- obs_FF + obs_FS + obs_SS  # Total individuals = 67

# Step 1: Calculate allele frequencies
total_alleles <- 2 * N
freq_F <- (2 * obs_FF + obs_FS) / total_alleles  # p
freq_S <- (obs_FS + 2 * obs_SS) / total_alleles  # q

cat("Allele Frequencies:\n")
cat(sprintf("p (F allele) = %.4f\n", freq_F))
cat(sprintf("q (S allele) = %.4f\n", freq_S))
cat(sprintf("p + q = %.4f\n\n", freq_F + freq_S))

# Step 2: Calculate expected genotype frequencies under HWE
exp_FF <- N * freq_F^2
exp_FS <- N * 2 * freq_F * freq_S
exp_SS <- N * freq_S^2

cat("Expected Genotype Counts (under HWE):\n")
cat(sprintf("FF: %.2f\n", exp_FF))
cat(sprintf("FS: %.2f\n", exp_FS))
cat(sprintf("SS: %.2f\n\n", exp_SS))

# Step 3: Chi-squared test using chisq.test()
observed <- c(obs_FF, obs_FS, obs_SS)
expected <- c(exp_FF, exp_FS, exp_SS)

# Create a summary table
results_table <- data.frame(
  Genotype = c("FF", "FS", "SS"),
  Observed = observed,
  Expected = round(expected, 2),
  Difference = observed - expected,
  Chi_sq_component = (observed - expected)^2 / expected
)

cat("Chi-Squared Analysis Table:\n")
print(results_table)
cat("\n")

# Perform chi-squared test
# Note: We use df = 1 because we estimated 1 parameter (p) from the data
chi_test <- chisq.test(observed, p = expected/N, rescale.p = TRUE)

cat("Chi-Squared Test Results:\n")
cat(sprintf("χ² statistic: %.4f\n", chi_test$statistic))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of freedom: %d\n", chi_test$parameter))
cat(sprintf("P-value: %.4f\n\n", chi_test$p.value))

# Alternative: Manual calculation
chi_sq_manual <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected)
p_value_manual <- pchisq(chi_sq_manual, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

cat("Manual Calculation (for verification):\n")
cat(sprintf("χ² statistic: %.4f\n", chi_sq_manual))
cat(sprintf("P-value (df=1): %.4f\n\n", p_value_manual))

# Conclusion
alpha <- 0.05
critical_value <- qchisq(1 - alpha, df = 1)

cat("Statistical Decision:\n")
cat(sprintf("Significance level (α): %.2f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Critical value (χ²₀.₀₅,₁): %.3f\n", critical_value))

if (chi_sq_manual < critical_value) {
  cat("\nConclusion: Fail to reject the null hypothesis.\n")
  cat("The population appears to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.\n")
} else {
  cat("\nConclusion: Reject the null hypothesis.\n")
  cat("The population shows significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.\n")
}
```
